texts: At a Cebuano café counter, ask whether the other person speaks Cebuano.
You missed what was said and ask for a repeat.
A simple opening question before you continue in Cebuano.
At a bright cafe counter, you first check whether the other person speaks Cebuano.

Hello / how are you. Kumusta is borrowed from Spanish cómo está and is shared with Tagalog, so it gives you a friendly entry point. The follow-up makasulti ka og Cebuano keeps the rest of the line clearly Cebuano (not Tagalog).
A bright cafe counter, a friendly first Cebuano question.
You missed what was said and ask for a repeat.
On the sidewalk, ask where the station is.
Sorry, I didn't understand. Please say it again.
A short apology plus a polite request to repeat.
Sorry, I didn't understand. Please say it again.
In the middle of the conversation, you make it clear you missed something and ask for a repeat.

Sorry. Pasaylo is the standard Cebuano apology — keep it instead of switching to a Tagalog form. Notice also the dual negation system: wala negates existence and past actions (wala ko kasabot, I didn't understand), while dili negates present and future verbs.
A short pause at the counter as you calmly ask for a repeat.
On the sidewalk, ask where the station is.
At a café counter, order one coffee politely.
Good day. Where is the station?
A warm greeting plus a simple where-question for a place.
Good day. Where is the station?
On the street, you ask for directions using asa and ang estasyon.
Where. Asa is the Cebuano where-word — clearly different from Tagalog saan. Cebuano also has no separate verb for "is" at A1, so Asa ang estasyon? is literally "Where the station?".
A bright street, a brief stop, a question about the station.
At a café counter, order one coffee politely.
In a small shop, ask the price of the item here.
A short, natural order at the cafe counter.
At the cafe, your order stays short and clear: one coffee, please.

Please. Palihug is the Cebuano polite-request word — different from Tagalog pakisuyo. Note the linker ka in usa ka kape: Cebuano connects a number to its noun with ka (one + linker + coffee), so "one coffee" needs all three pieces.
A cafe counter, a simple order with a friendly please.
In a small shop, ask the price of the item here.
At a station, ask when the train arrives.
A very short price question about a visible item.
In a small shop, you point at the item and ask: tagpila ni?

How much (price). Tagpila is the Cebuano price question — different from Tagalog magkano. The root pila means "how much/many" generally (like Tagalog ilan), and the tag- prefix turns it into a price-specific ask.
A small shop, a visible item, a short question about the price.
At a station, ask when the train arrives.
At a pharmacy or help desk, say that you need help.
A simple time question at the station.
At the station, you look down the rails and ask when the train will arrive.
When. Kanus-a is the Cebuano when-word — clearly different from Tagalog kailan. Keep the hyphen in standard writing; you will also see kanusa without the hyphen in casual text.
A station, an arrival board, a simple when-question.
At a pharmacy or help desk, say that you need help.
Inside a café or shop, make a short positive comment.
A direct request for help in a service situation.
At a pharmacy or help desk, you make it clear that you need help.

Help. Two small Cebuano grammar pieces ride along: ko is a short pronoun ("I/my") that always comes after the verb, and og marks what comes next as the object of need. Together they let you build short, natural A1 requests without a separate "for" word.
An information desk or pharmacy, a clear request for help.
Inside a café or shop, make a short positive comment.
Confirm a simple plan for tomorrow at seven.
A short positive small-talk line about the place.
Inside the cafe, you drop in one warm line: nindot dinhi.

Nice / lovely. Nindot is the everyday Cebuano compliment word — different from Tagalog maganda. Notice there is no "is" verb: Nindot dinhi is literally "Nice here", and Cebuano at A1 simply skips the copula.
A bright, pleasant spot, a short positive comment.
Confirm a simple plan for tomorrow at seven.
Close the interaction with thanks and goodbye.
A short confirmation for a plan the next day.
Settling the plan, you agree: tomorrow at seven, sige.

Tomorrow. Ugma is the Cebuano word — different from Tagalog bukas. Times of day use the Spanish-borrowed alas system (alas siyete = seven o'clock), which Cebuano shares with Tagalog and Philippine English.
A quick plan, a time, and a friendly nod of agreement.
Close the interaction with thanks and goodbye.
You have completed Cebuano A1 Practical 1.
A short thanks plus farewell at the end of a help interaction.
After the help, you say salamat kaayo and head off on a warm note.

Thank you. Salamat is shared with Tagalog (and ultimately from Arabic salama), so it travels well across the Philippines. The intensifier kaayo ("very") and the casual babay keep the close-out feeling natural in Cebuano.
A wrap-up at the counter, a thanks and a short goodbye.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
At a counter, admit that you do not understand and ask for simple help.
Ask someone to write the information down.
I don't understand. Please help me.
A clear repair phrase that opens up help, not just a repeat.
I don't understand. Please help me.
At the shop, you make it clear that you missed something and ask for simple help.

Understand / get it. Kasabot is the Cebuano anchor — different from Tagalog naiintindihan. Note Cebuano's two negators: wala covers existence and past-style states (wala ko kasabot, I don't understand), while dili negates present and future verbs and adjectives.
A service counter, a short pause, the learner asks for simple help.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask someone to write the information down.
Ask someone to show a location on a map or phone.
A practical request for numbers, addresses, or names.
At the desk, you ask for the detail to be written down so you can see it.

Write it down. Isulat is the i- request form built from the root sulat (write/letter). Cebuano verbs don't conjugate for person, so the same form works whether you, the cashier, or anyone else does the writing.
A small desk, pen and paper, a request to write it down.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask someone to show a location on a map or phone.
Ask for a binary choice between two visible options.
Show me on the map, please.
A visual repair when spoken directions are too hard to follow.
Show me on the map, please.
With the phone map open, you signal that you want to see the place pointed out.
Map. Mapa is a Spanish-loan everyday anchor used for both paper and phone maps. The marker sa here means "on/in/at" — Cebuano uses the same little word for many location and object cues.
A phone map on a counter, a finger pointing at a location.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask for a binary choice between two visible options.
Ask whether the visible item is available or in stock.
A very short choice question for two visible things.
Two items are in view, and you ask: this one or that one.

That one. Cebuano demonstratives map to distance from the speaker: kani is close to me, kana is close to you, kadto is far from both. The pairing kani o kana is a clean A1 way to point and choose without naming the item.
Two visible options on a counter, the learner asks this one or that one.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask whether the visible item is available or in stock.
Ask whether card payment is accepted.
A short shop question when you point at an item.
You point at the item in the shop and ask whether they have any of it.
Have / there is. Naa is the Cebuano existence word — different from Tagalog meron / mayroon. The negative pair is wala for "none / don't have."
A small shop shelf, a visible item, a short availability question.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask whether card payment is accepted.
Ask for a receipt and, if useful, a paper bag.
A direct payment question before you head to the register.
At the cashier, you check ahead whether they take card.
Accept / take. Dawat is the Cebuano root; the mu- prefix marks an active non-past verb (mudawat = does/will accept), and the little og marks kard as the object being accepted.
A cash register and card terminal, a short payment question.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Ask for a receipt and, if useful, a paper bag.
Announce that you have a booking under a name.
A checkout request for the receipt and wrapping.
After paying, you ask for a receipt and a bag in one short line.
Receipt. Resibo is a Spanish-loan checkout word, and supot is the everyday word for a shopping bag.
A checkout counter, a printed receipt, a small paper bag.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Announce that you have a booking under a name.
Confirm that the item, vehicle, or place is the correct one.
I have a booking under the name Ana.
A short check-in line for a hotel, restaurant, or appointment.
I have a booking under the name Ana.
At a hotel or restaurant, you arrive and state the booking under the name Ana.

Name. Ngalan is the Cebuano word for name — different from Tagalog pangalan. Note the marker ni in front of a personal name (ni Ana = of Ana / Ana's), which Cebuano uses for the named possessor of the booking.
A reception desk, a name on the booking, the learner checks in.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
Confirm that the item, vehicle, or place is the correct one.
A safety-check question before you board, buy, or step inside.
it is / that is the one
At the vehicle or door, you double-check first: is this the right one?

Right / correct. Husto is the everyday Cebuano confirmation word. Mao acts like a soft "is/that" identifier, and ang is the focus marker that makes ang husto behave like "the right one" — Cebuano has no separate verb "to be" at A1.
A door or vehicle sign, the learner confirms it is the right one.
Short repairs and service questions in Cebuano
You have completed Cebuano A1 Practical 2.
A short request for a pause in an ongoing situation.
You have something to dig out of your wallet, so you ask for a brief wait.
A moment / briefly. Kadiyot is the Cebuano short-time anchor — different from Tagalog sandali. The casual spoken form kadyot drops the middle vowel; both are accepted.
A checkout pause, the learner asks for a brief wait.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
At a street corner, ask whether to go right or left.
While navigating, ask if the place is far to walk.
To the right or to the left?
A short directions question when two ways are possible.
To the right or to the left?
At the corner, you ask whether the right way is to the right or to the left.
Right. Tuo is the Cebuano word for the right side — note that wala here means "left" (a different sense from wala as the negator "none / not"). Cebuano context tells you which one is meant.
A street corner with two clear direction choices.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
While navigating, ask if the place is far to walk.
Outside a shop or office, check if it is open now.
A simple question before you decide whether to walk.
On the street, you size up the distance before you start walking.
Far. Layo is the everyday Cebuano distance word — the same in Tagalog, so it travels well. The little ba turns a statement into a yes/no question, which is the standard A1 way to ask.
A sidewalk route check before walking farther.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
Outside a shop or office, check if it is open now.
At a bus stop, ask which bus goes toward the market.
A short question at a door, counter, or shopfront.
In front of the shop, you check first whether it is open right now.
Open. Abli is the Cebuano word for open, different from Tagalog bukas (which in Tagalog also means "tomorrow"). Pair it with karon (now) for a clean A1 opening-hours check.
A shop door, an open sign, the learner checks before entering.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
At a bus stop, ask which bus goes toward the market.
On a bus, confirm whether this is the next stop.
Which bus goes to the market?
A practical question when several buses are possible.
Which bus goes to the market?
At the stop, many buses pass and you ask which one is heading to the market.

Heading to. Paingon is the Cebuano direction anchor for transit and destinations, and it pairs with unsang (which) — note unsa/unsang is Cebuano while Tagalog uses ano/anong. Merkado is a Spanish-loan everyday word for market.
A bus stop with route signs toward the market.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
On a bus, confirm whether this is the next stop.
At a transit counter, buy one ticket toward Cebu.
A safety check just before you get off.
Inside the bus, you make sure this is the next stop.

Next / following. Sunod carries the practical idea of "next in line" and works for stops, turns, and orders. The little nga is the Cebuano linker that joins a modifier (sunod) to its noun (hunonganan).
Inside a bus approaching the next stop.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
At a transit counter, buy one ticket toward Cebu.
Outside a place, ask what time it closes.
A short order for a counter, port, or bus station.
At the terminal, you buy one ticket bound for Cebu.

Ticket. Tiket is the everyday Cebuano spelling, and ticket is accepted too. Note the counting pattern usa ka — Cebuano links a number to its noun with the little ka, so it is literally "one piece-of ticket."
A transit counter with one ticket to Cebu.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
Outside a place, ask what time it closes.
Use a street corner as the landmark and turn right.
A short planning question outside a shop, museum, or office.
Outside the museum or shop, you ask the closing time.

Closes / will close. Mosira is built from the root sira (close) with the mu- prefix that marks an active, non-past Cebuano verb. Unsang orasa uses the Cebuano question word unsa (Tagalog would say anong oras).
A door hours sign, the learner asks the closing time.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
Use a street corner as the landmark and turn right.
Choose between walking and taking a taxi.
A short direction with a visible landmark.
You spot the corner and say to turn right there.
Corner. Eskina is a Spanish-loan landmark word used every day in Cebuano directions. The little sa marks location ("at the corner"), the same particle you use for destinations and many object cues.
A street corner landmark with a right turn.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
Choose between walking and taking a taxi.
Say that you went past the stop and need to recover.
Shall we walk or take a taxi?
A short decision between two ways of getting around.
Shall we walk or take a taxi?
On the side of the road, you and your friend pick between walking and taking a taxi.

Walk. Lakaw is the Cebuano root for walking; the mag- prefix turns it into a shared we-action (maglakaw = let's walk), with ta as the inclusive we. The same mag- shape stacks onto taksi to mean "take a taxi."
A sidewalk decision between walking and taking a taxi.
Ways, times, and transit in Cebuano
Say that you went past the stop and need to recover.
You have completed Cebuano A1 Practical 3.
A short sentence when you have missed a stop.
Right after passing the stop, you make it clear that you need help with the next step.

Went past. Milapas is built from the root lapas (past / beyond) with the mi- prefix that marks a completed Cebuano action. The little ko means "I" — Cebuano verbs do not change for person, so the same milapas works for siya (he/she) or sila (they).
The bus has passed the stop, the learner explains what happened.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
At a small restaurant, ask for a table for two people.
After sitting down, ask for the menu.
A short request at the entrance of a restaurant or café.
At a small eatery, you ask for a table for two.

Table. Lamesa is a Spanish-loan word (from "la mesa") shared with Tagalog, so it travels easily. Pair it with palihug (the Cebuano "please," different from Tagalog pakisuyo) for a polite arrival line.
A small restaurant host stand with two guests.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
After sitting down, ask for the menu.
Before ordering food, ask for water for now.
A very short request when you cannot order yet.
After you sit down, you ask for a menu in a polite way.
Menu. Menu is the everyday loanword that works the same in Cebuano and English. The polite touch comes from palihug — the Cebuano "please," not Tagalog pakisuyo.
A table setting with a server bringing a menu.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
Before ordering food, ask for water for now.
Ordering a drink, ask for it without sugar.
A safe first order while you are still deciding.
Before you choose any food, you ask for just water for now.
Water. Tubig is a core Cebuano word that is the same in Tagalog, so it carries across the Philippines. The little lang sa softens the order to "just... for now," a useful A1 hedge.
A glass of water ordered before food.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
Ordering a drink, ask for it without sugar.
At a food stall, ask if the item is fresh.
A simple tweak for coffee, tea, or juice.
When ordering coffee, you make it clear that you want no sugar.

Sugar. Asukar is a Spanish-loan word (from "azúcar") shared with Tagalog, easy to remember. Walay is the Cebuano "none / there is no," used to subtract things from an order — the everyday counterpart to Tagalog walang.
A coffee cup beside a sugar bowl crossed out.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
At a food stall, ask if the item is fresh.
At the table, ask for more water.
A short question before buying or tasting.
At the food stall, you ask whether this is fresh.
Fresh. Presko is a Spanish-loan word (from "fresco") shared with Tagalog and instantly useful at any food stall. The little ba turns the statement into a yes/no question — the everyday A1 pattern.
A food stall with fresh produce on display.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
At the table, ask for more water.
At a counter, ask whether the food can be taken away.
A simple refill request when your glass is empty.
The glass is empty, so you ask for more water.

More / extra. Dugang lets you extend any order without learning new sentence structure — just put it in front of the noun. It is the Cebuano word, where Tagalog typically uses dagdag for the same idea.
An empty glass at a café table.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
At a counter, ask whether the food can be taken away.
During a meal, say that this is very tasty.
Can I take this to go?
A short question when you do not want to eat in.
Can I take this to go?
At the counter, you ask whether this can be taken away.

To take (away). Dad-on is the Cebuano verb for carrying something off, useful for food, packages, and small purchases. The pair mahimo ba sets up a polite "is it possible to..." opener common in shops and cafés.
A takeaway counter with packed food.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
During a meal, say that this is very tasty.
When the server asks if you need anything else, say that this is enough for now.
A friendly comment on food or a drink.
After you taste, you say that this is really tasty.
Tasty. Lami is the Cebuano word for "delicious / good-tasting," where Tagalog typically uses masarap. Adding kaayo after it intensifies to "really" — a classic Cebuano "adjective + kaayo" pattern.
A meal tasting moment with a positive reaction.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
When the server asks if you need anything else, say that this is enough for now.
At the end of the meal, ask for the bill.
That is all for now, thank you.
A short reply when you do not need anything else yet.
That is all for now, thank you.
The server asks if you want more, and you reply that this is all for now.
Mao lang sa is a natural short way to say that is all for now.
A server checking whether anything else is needed.
Café, food, and small shop questions in Cebuano
At the end of the meal, ask for the bill.
You have completed Cebuano A1 Practical 4.
A direct request when you are ready to pay.
After the meal, you ask for the bill so you can pay.
Bill / amount to pay. Bayranan is built from the Cebuano root bayad ("pay") plus a noun-forming ending — the thing that is to be paid. The little ang marks it as the focus of the request.
End of meal, bill folder on the table.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Arriving to meet someone, say that you are a little late.
You have met before but forgot the person’s name.
A short apology line without a long explanation.
You arrive at the meeting spot and clearly say you are a little late.
To be running late. Naulahi is the Cebuano "I was late," where Tagalog usually says nahuli. Pair it with gamay ("a little") for a soft, A1-friendly apology that needs no extra reason.
Arriving a little late to meet someone.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
You have met before but forgot the person’s name.
Ask what someone is called in a casual setting.
A direct repair line when you can't recall someone's name.
When you start chatting again, you honestly admit that you have forgotten the person’s name.
To have forgotten. Nakalimot is the Cebuano social-repair word, where Tagalog uses nakalimutan. Pair it with ngalan ("name" in Cebuano, where Tagalog says pangalan) for a clean, honest A1 fix.
A friendly moment after forgetting a name.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Ask what someone is called in a casual setting.
After an introduction, say you are pleased that you met.
A short question for when you need the person's name.
Meeting someone new, you ask what you should call them.

Call / to call. Tawag is the core Cebuano word for naming or calling someone, where Tagalog also uses tawag in the same way. The question word unsa ("what") is Cebuano, distinct from Tagalog ano — a key A1 marker.
A casual introduction with a name question.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
After an introduction, say you are pleased that you met.
Ask if someone is from Cebu.
A warm reply after an introduction.
After the introductions, you say that you are glad you met.
To be glad. Nalipay is the Cebuano "I was happy," while Tagalog uses natuwa or masaya. The little nga is the Cebuano linker between clauses — handy any time you want to say "that..." after a feeling.
A warm first meeting after introductions.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Ask if someone is from Cebu.
A short where-from question without a long life story.
Meeting someone new, you ask whether they are from Cebu.
From (a place). Taga is the same in Cebuano and Tagalog, so this anchor travels easily across the Philippines. Just put a city, island, or area right after it — taga Cebu, taga Davao, taga diri.
A casual question about being from Cebu.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Ask if someone is free tonight.
A short question about where someone currently lives.
Standing nearby, you ask the person whether they live around here.

To live (somewhere). Nagpuyo uses the Cebuano nag- aspect prefix to mean "is living," while Tagalog typically uses nakatira. Diri is the Cebuano "here," distinct from Tagalog dito — a tiny word, but a clear giveaway you are speaking Cebuano.
A neighborhood conversation about living nearby.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Ask if someone is free tonight.
A casual question before you suggest a small plan.
While making plans, you ask whether the person is free tonight.
Evening / night. Gabii is the Cebuano time word, where Tagalog uses gabi. Libre is a Spanish-loan word (from "libre") shared with Tagalog, meaning "free / available" — a quick way to ask about plans.
An evening plan question in a casual chat.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Answer a plan softly with maybe later.
Shall we meet at the park?
A short suggestion with a specific meeting spot.
Shall we meet at the park?
After asking about the time, you suggest meeting at the park.
Park. Parke is a Spanish-loan word (from "parque") shared with Tagalog, easy to spot. The mag- prefix plus ta turns magkita ta into the Cebuano "let's meet" — a quick A1 plan-making move.
A simple plan to meet at the park.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
Answer a plan softly with maybe later.
End a casual meeting with take care.
A short reply when you don't want to commit yet.
The plan isn't set yet, so you reply with a casual maybe later.
Maybe. Tingali is the Cebuano hedge, where Tagalog usually says siguro. Pair it with unya ("later" in Cebuano, where Tagalog uses mamaya) for a soft, friendly non-commitment.
A casual maybe-later reply to a plan.
Getting to know people and small plans in Cebuano
End a casual meeting with take care.
You have completed Cebuano A1 Practical 5.
A friendly goodbye at the end of a meeting.
At the end of the meeting, you say "always take care."
Take care. Amping is the warm Cebuano goodbye, where Tagalog typically says ingat. Pirmi ("always" in Cebuano, distinct from Tagalog palagi) adds a sweet little flourish to the sign-off.
A friendly goodbye after a casual meeting.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
You feel unwell and need to say it simply.
Ask whether there is a pharmacy nearby.
A simple status update with no diagnosis or long explanation.
With a small body niggle, you simply say you are not feeling well.
Feeling / how one feels. Pamati is the Cebuano word for your bodily state, where Tagalog usually says pakiramdam. Pair it with lain ("off") for an honest A1 health check-in without naming a sickness.
Person sitting down and saying they do not feel well.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Ask whether there is a pharmacy nearby.
At a pharmacy, say that you need medicine.
A practical question for finding the right spot for small health needs.
On the street, you ask whether there is a pharmacy nearby.

Pharmacy. Botika is a Spanish loanword (from botica) used widely across Cebuano and Tagalog alike. The Cebuano existential naay ("there is") is distinct from Tagalog meron — use it for any "is there a ... nearby?" question.
Looking for a nearby pharmacy on the street.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
At a pharmacy, say that you need medicine.
Point to a place and say it hurts here.
A short need-line, no dosage or medical advice.
At the pharmacy, you clearly say you need medicine.

Medicine. Tambal is the Cebuano word, while Tagalog uses gamot for the same idea. The little og before tambal is the Cebuano object marker for non-specific items — Tagalog usually drops the marker here.
Asking for medicine at a pharmacy counter.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Point to a place and say it hurts here.
A minimal pain note, used when pointing says more than words.
You point to a spot on your body and say it hurts here.
Pain / sore. Sakit is shared with Tagalog (masakit), but the Cebuano locative diri ("here") is different from Tagalog dito. Pointing plus sakit diri is all you need at A1 to signal where it hurts.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Say that you need to drink water.
A concrete A1 complaint, with no cause or treatment to explain.
You let someone know your head aches, with no extra medical detail.

Head. Ulo is the same word in Cebuano and Tagalog, but Cebuano builds the headache phrase as labad akong ulo, where Tagalog typically says masakit ang ulo ko. The little akong is Cebuano for "my" — Tagalog uses ko after the noun.
Holding head gently during a headache.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Say that you need to drink water.
Ask whether there is a doctor here.
A small body need, kept fresh by spotlighting the verb instead of water.
On a hot day or after some effort, you say you need to drink water.

To drink. Moinom is the Cebuano mu-/mo- future-action form of inom, where Tagalog uses iinom for the same idea. The prefix mo- marks an upcoming or intended action — a core A1 building block in Cebuano.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Ask whether there is a doctor here.
Say that you have a peanut allergy.
A clear question for a person, without claiming an emergency or diagnosis.
If medical help is needed, you ask whether there is a doctor here.

Doctor. Doktor is a Spanish-origin word shared by Cebuano and Tagalog, easy to recognise at A1. Cebuano builds the question with naay ("there is"), whereas Tagalog uses meron — the verb-first shape stays the same.
Asking whether a doctor is nearby.
Health, pharmacy and small needs in Cebuano
Say that you have a peanut allergy.
Ask someone to call for help.
An important food or medicine boundary, with no extra detail.
With food or medicine, you clearly say: I am allergic to peanuts.
Alerdyik is the adjective for saying that you are allergic; sa mani names peanuts as the allergen.
Pointing out a peanut allergy before eating.

Ask someone to call for help.
